summary: Defines how an SNMP notification (a trap or inform message) is translated into a syslog message. This lets a device that speaks SNMP have its events show up in ordinary syslog collectors in a predictable format. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: One machine shouts alerts in one language and another writes them in a diary in a different language. This document is the translation guide, so an alert from the first can be written down properly in the second.

subtitle: How an SNMP trap or inform becomes exactly one SYSLOG message without losing its contents.

tldr.problem: Some sites want every event notification to arrive through a single management protocol, but devices send SNMP notifications while collectors may only speak SYSLOG.
tldr.mechanism: A translator maps each SNMP notification to one SYSLOG message and carries the notification's variable bindings in a new structured data element with the SD-ID snmp.
tldr.outcome: Operators get SNMP events in SYSLOG collectors in a predictable format, though long notifications may be truncated and access control must be kept consistent.

facts.label: Mapping ratio
facts.value: One SNMP notification to one SYSLOG message

today: RFC 5675 is a Proposed Standard from October 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the SYSLOG protocol in RFC 5424 and has a companion in RFC 5676.

sections.title: Why Translate Notifications
sections.content:
SNMP and SYSLOG are two widely used protocols for event notifications. Some environments require that all notifications be collected by one system daemon, such as a SYSLOG collector or an SNMP notification receiver, through a single management protocol. In those environments, notifications must be translated from one protocol to the other.

The newer SYSLOG protocol in RFC 5424 supports structured data elements, which makes it possible to map in both directions without losing information. This RFC specifies a concrete mapping from SNMP notifications (RFC 3416) into SYSLOG messages, and defines one new structured data element to carry the PDU portion of the notification.

The system doing the work is called an SNMP-to-SYSLOG translator. It runs an SNMP notification receiver and a SYSLOG originator.
sections.eli5: Some offices want all their alarm messages in one notebook. Alarms that come in one language need to be rewritten into the notebook's language first.

sections.title: SNMP Notifications and the Translator
sections.content:
SNMP has two notification operations: SNMPv2-Trap-PDU, an unconfirmed delivery mechanism, and InformRequest-PDU, a confirmed one. Both carry the same structure: a request-id, two ignored integers (error-status and error-index) and a list of variable bindings. The first two variable bindings are always sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0, followed by the variables named in the notification definition and any extras the sender adds. For SNMPv3, the data is wrapped in a scopedPDU with a contextEngineID and a contextName.

The mapping assumes the RFC 3416 format. Notifications in the SNMPv1 format must be translated as described in Section 3.1 of RFC 3584 first. Implementations MUST drop invalid SNMP messages before they reach the translator.

Every SNMP notification maps to exactly one SYSLOG message. The translator is not transparent to the collector: the SYSLOG header describes the translator's own system, such as its hostname and timestamp, while the notification's data sits in the structured data.
sections.eli5: An alarm is a note with a number of facts on it. The translator copies all the facts onto a new note, but the new note carries the translator's own name and the time it was written.

sections.title: The SYSLOG Header and MSG Part
sections.content:
The translator fills the VERSION, TIMESTAMP, HOSTNAME, APP-NAME, PROCID and MSGID fields with values specific to its own system. The header character set MUST be seven-bit ASCII in an eight-bit field.

By default the facility SHOULD be 3 (messages generated by system daemons) and the severity SHOULD be 5 ("Notice: normal but significant condition"). A translator that understands the type of notification it received might choose other values.

The MSG part is optional and may hold a free-form textual description of the event. Per RFC 5424 it SHOULD be Unicode encoded as UTF-8, but if the originator cannot do that it MAY use another encoding.
sections.eli5: The top of the new note says who wrote it and how important it is. Unless told otherwise, the translator marks the note as an ordinary, noteworthy event.

sections.title: The snmp Structured Data Element
sections.content:
The new SD-ID is snmp. For an SNMPv3 notification, the element starts with ctxEngine (the contextEngineID as a hexadecimal string) and ctxName (the contextName as a UTF-8 string); both MUST be present. The remaining parameters correspond to the variable bindings, numbered from 1 in their order in the notification.

For binding N, a vN parameter carries the name as a dotted OID. The value goes in a parameter whose first letter shows its SNMP type, for example oN for an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, xN for an OCTET STRING in hex, cN for a Counter32, dN for a signed integer and iN for an IpAddress.

A MIB-aware implementation may add an lN parameter with the object's label and an aN parameter with an alternate textual form of the value. These make messages easier to read but longer, which may cause SYSLOG messages to be truncated, so implementations SHOULD let the operator turn them on and off. The SYSLOG message may also contain other structured data elements. For the origin SD-ID, the ip parameter MAY come from the snmpTrapAddress varbind and enterpriseId MAY be taken from snmpTrapOID.
sections.eli5: Each fact in the alarm gets a short label such as v1, v2, v3 and a letter that says what kind of fact it is, such as a number or a name. That way anyone can rebuild the original alarm.

sections.title: Worked Example: A linkUp Trap
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an SNMPv3 linkUp trap, defined in RFC 2863 with the objects ifIndex, ifAdminStatus and ifOperStatus. The request-id is 7145575, and the trap reports ifIndex 3 with both statuses up(1).

The SYSLOG result has priority <29>, which is facility 3 and severity 5, version 1, the host mymachine.example.com, the application snmptrapd and the MSGID ID47. Its single structured data element has SD-ID snmp, context engine 800002b804616263 and context name ctx1. Variable bindings 1 and 2 are sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0, and the value of the latter, 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.4, identifies the linkUp trap.
sections.eli5: A pretend alarm says that network plug number 3 is now working. The translator writes it as a short list with an ID, a value and a plain-English label for each fact.

sections.title: Tunnelling With the SYSLOG-MSG-MIB
sections.content:
A companion document, RFC 5676, defines a MIB module that represents SYSLOG messages and sends them as SNMP notifications. Used together with this mapping, the two can build forwarding chains in either direction. A collector can translate SYSLOG messages that contain SNMP notifications back into the original notifications, which is called tunnelling SNMP through SYSLOG. Conversely, an SNMP application can emit SYSLOG messages recorded in the MIB.

Because SYSLOG transports have size restrictions and the SYSLOG encoding is more verbose, a tunnelled SNMP notification can be truncated and arrive incomplete. In the other direction, if parameters are missing from a syslogMsgNotification, a forwarding application MUST retrieve them from the SYSLOG-MSG-MIB. Regular polling of the MIB can cover lost notifications.
sections.eli5: You can send the alarm through the diary system and turn it back into an alarm later. Sometimes the diary page is too small, so a few details might get cut off.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5424 apply. In addition, SNMP has access control that makes sure notifications go only to authorized receivers. Operators who use this mapping should enforce a consistent policy so that nobody can read through SYSLOG a notification they could not have read through SNMP.

IANA registered the SD-ID snmp, with its optional PARAM-NAMEs (ctxEngine, ctxName and the position-numbered v, l, o, x, c, C, u, d, i, n, p, t and a parameters), in the SYSLOG Structured Data ID Values registry.
sections.eli5: If a secret alarm was only meant for certain people, copying it into the diary must not let everyone read it.
